source_refs.note: Chapter 19 exercise (PDF 56-58), solved: 9 MCQs keyed with reasons (no key is printed), 9 short-answer, 4 constructed-response and 4 descriptive questions. MCQ III, VI, Short a and Q7 (meso lactic acid) carry Book corrections.

blocks.prompt: I) Which of the following is organic in nature?
blocks.explanation: Some simple carbon compounds are traditionally inorganic and excluded from organic chemistry: carbonates, cyanides (HCN), CO₂, CO (and CS₂). CCl₄ (tetrachloromethane) is an organic halogen compound (a haloalkane).

blocks.prompt: II) The empirical formula of CH₃CH₂CH=CH₂ matches with:
blocks.explanation:
CH₃CH₂CH=CH₂ = C₄H₈ → empirical formula CH₂.
CH₃CH₃ = C₂H₆ → CH₃
CH₂=CHCH₃ = C₃H₆ → CH₂ ✓
CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃ = C₄H₁₀ → C₂H₅
CH≡CH = C₂H₂ → CH

blocks.prompt: III) Compounds having single bonds usually undergo reactions:
blocks.explanation: Saturated compounds (only single bonds) cannot add atoms without breaking a bond, so they usually react by substitution, e.g. CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl; CH₃CH₂Br + KOH(aq) → CH₃CH₂OH + KBr. Addition needs a double or triple bond.

blocks.prompt: IV) The functional group present in urea (H₂N–C(=O)–NH₂) is:
blocks.explanation: In urea the C=O group is bonded to –NH₂, i.e. –C(=O)–NH₂, the acid amide group. The carbonyl and amino parts together make up this one functional group, which behaves differently from a separate C=O or –NH₂.

blocks.prompt: V) Which molecule is chiral and can rotate the plane polarised light?
blocks.explanation: Pentan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₂CH₃: C-2 carries four different groups (H, OH, CH₃, C₃H₇), so it is chiral. The others have no carbon with four different groups (2-methylbutan-2-ol has two CH₃ on C-2).

blocks.prompt: VI) Which carbon in CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH(OH)CH₃ is chiral?
blocks.explanation:
IUPAC name: 4-methylpentan-2-ol (numbered from the end nearer the OH).
C-2, CH(OH), carries H, OH, CH₃ and CH₂CH(CH₃)₂: four different groups → chiral.
C-4, CH(CH₃), carries two CH₃ groups → not chiral. See the Book correction about numbering.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The answer depends on how the chain is numbered. By IUPAC numbering (4-methylpentan-2-ol) the chiral carbon is C-2, keyed (b). Counted from the left of the formula as printed it is the 4th carbon, so (d) is also arguable. The question should name the numbering.

blocks.prompt: VII) In what ways could two compounds of molecular formula C₂H₂Br₂ be related to each other?
blocks.explanation: C₂H₂Br₂ can be CH₂=CBr₂ (1,1-dibromoethene) or CHBr=CHBr (1,2-dibromoethene). 1,1- and 1,2- are constitutional isomers; 1,2-dibromoethene exists as cis and trans isomers. No carbon has four different groups, so there are no optical isomers.

blocks.prompt: VIII) Which of following shows cis-trans isomerism?
blocks.explanation: 2-Butene, CH₃CH=CHCH₃: each doubly bonded carbon has two different groups (H and CH₃), so cis and trans forms exist. In the others one double-bond carbon carries two identical groups (=CH₂ or =CCl₂).

blocks.prompt: IX) Which one of the following pairs do the isomers have identical boiling points?
blocks.explanation: Enantiomers have identical physical and chemical properties (boiling point, melting point, density) except the direction in which they rotate plane-polarized light. Cis-trans and structural isomers have different boiling points.

blocks.prompt: a) Define enantioers. Give enantiomers of 2-methylbutan-2-ol.
blocks.explanation:
Enantiomers are stereoisomers that are non-superimposable mirror images of each other. They have identical properties but rotate plane-polarized light equally in opposite directions, (+) and (−).
2-Methylbutan-2-ol, CH₃CH₂C(OH)(CH₃)₂, has no chiral carbon (C-2 carries two CH₃ groups), so it has no enantiomers (see the Book correction). Its isomer 2-methylbutan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂OH, has a chiral C-2 (H, CH₃, C₂H₅, CH₂OH) and exists as (+) and (−) enantiomers, mirror images of each other about C-2.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: “enantioers” is a misprint for “enantiomers”. 2-Methylbutan-2-ol is achiral (MCQ V uses it as the achiral option), so it has no enantiomers. A chiral isomer such as 2-methylbutan-1-ol (or butan-2-ol) was probably meant.

blocks.prompt: b) Alkanes have no functional group. Justify.
blocks.explanation: A functional group is an atom, group of atoms or multiple bond that gives a compound its characteristic properties. Alkanes contain only C–C and C–H single (σ) bonds; they have no polar bond, no charge and no double or triple bond, so they have no functional group. This is why they are unreactive and cannot form hydrogen bonds.

blocks.prompt:
c) Deduce the empirical and molecular formulae of the following compounds.
a) [drawn: a six-membered ring of single bonds]  b) [drawn: a zig-zag chain of five carbons with two double bonds, second-third and fourth-fifth carbon from the left]  c) [drawn: a four-membered ring (square) with double bonds on two opposite sides]
blocks.explanation:
a) Cyclohexane (ring of 6 CH₂): molecular formula C₆H₁₂; empirical formula CH₂.
b) CH₃–CH=CH–CH=CH₂ (penta-1,3-diene): molecular formula C₅H₈; empirical formula C₅H₈ (5 : 8 cannot be simplified).
c) Cyclobutadiene (4 CH in a ring): molecular formula C₄H₄; empirical formula CH.

blocks.prompt:
d) Give systematic names of the following compounds.
i) CH₃-CH₂-CN  ii) CH₃COCH₂CH₂-CH₃  iii) CH₃CH₂COOCH₃
blocks.explanation:
i) CH₃CH₂CN: propanenitrile (3 carbons including the C of CN)
ii) CH₃COCH₂CH₂CH₃: pentan-2-one
iii) CH₃CH₂COOCH₃: methyl propanoate

blocks.prompt: e) Define electrophile and nucleophile with two examples each.
blocks.explanation:
Electrophile (electron lover): an atom or group that accepts a pair of electrons to form a new bond; positive ions or neutral molecules, e.g. H⁺, NO₂⁺ (also Br⁺, CH₃⁺, SO₃, BF₃).
Nucleophile (nucleus lover): an atom or group that donates a pair of electrons to form a new bond; negative ions or neutral molecules with lone pairs, e.g. OH⁻, NH₃ (also CN⁻, Br⁻, H₂O).

blocks.prompt: f) Pent-2-ene shows cis-trans isomerism but pent-1-ene does not. Give reason.
blocks.explanation: Cis-trans isomerism needs two different groups on each doubly bonded carbon. Pent-2-ene, CH₃–CH=CH–CH₂CH₃: C-2 has H and CH₃, C-3 has H and C₂H₅, so cis and trans forms exist. Pent-1-ene, CH₂=CH–CH₂CH₂CH₃: C-1 carries two identical H atoms, so exchanging positions gives the same molecule; no cis-trans isomers.

blocks.prompt:
g) Define:
i) Constitutional isomerism  ii) Stereoisomerism
blocks.explanation:
i) Constitutional (structural) isomerism: compounds with the same molecular formula but different connection (sequence) of atoms, e.g. ethanol CH₃CH₂OH and methoxymethane CH₃OCH₃ (C₂H₆O).
ii) Stereoisomerism: compounds with the same molecular formula and the same connection of atoms but a different arrangement of atoms in space (configuration); it is of two types, optical and cis-trans isomerism.

blocks.prompt:
h) Define:
i) racemic mixture  ii) Optical activity
blocks.explanation:
i) Racemic mixture: a mixture of equal amounts (50 : 50) of the dextrorotatory (+) and laevorotatory (−) enantiomers; it is optically inactive and written as (±), e.g. (±)-lactic acid.
ii) Optical activity: the ability of a compound to rotate the plane of plane-polarized light, to the right (dextrorotatory, +) or to the left (laevorotatory, −); it is measured with a polarimeter.

blocks.prompt: i Explain why meso tartaric acid is optically inactive although it has two chiral carbon atoms.
blocks.explanation: Meso-tartaric acid, HOOC–CH(OH)–CH(OH)–COOH, has two similar chiral carbons with opposite configurations and a plane of symmetry through the middle of the molecule. One half is the mirror image of the other; each half rotates plane-polarized light equally in opposite directions, so the rotation is cancelled within the molecule (internal compensation). Hence it is optically inactive.

blocks.prompt: a) A compound C₆H₅CH₃ reacts with Cl₂ in the presence of sunlight to form the product C₆H₅CCl₃.Name the mechanism of the reaction. Give its different steps.
blocks.explanation:
Mechanism: free radical substitution (in the side chain), through homolysis of Cl₂ in sunlight.
Overall: C₆H₅CH₃ + 3Cl₂ → C₆H₅CCl₃ + 3HCl (sunlight)
1. Initiation: Cl–Cl → Cl• + •Cl (sunlight, homolytic fission)
2. Propagation (chain steps):
C₆H₅CH₃ + Cl• → C₆H₅CH₂• + HCl
C₆H₅CH₂• + Cl₂ → C₆H₅CH₂Cl + Cl•
The Cl• formed repeats the cycle, replacing the side-chain H atoms one by one: C₆H₅CH₂Cl → C₆H₅CHCl₂ → C₆H₅CCl₃.
3. Termination (radicals combine):
Cl• + Cl• → Cl₂
C₆H₅CH₂• + Cl• → C₆H₅CH₂Cl
C₆H₅CH₂• + •CH₂C₆H₅ → C₆H₅CH₂CH₂C₆H₅
The ring H atoms are not replaced under these conditions; this is the same initiation → propagation → termination pathway as CH₄ + 4Cl₂ → CCl₄ + 4HCl.

blocks.prompt:
b) Draw the mirror image of each of the following compounds. Label each molecule as chiral or achiral.
i) 2-bromo-2-chloropropane  ii) 1-bromo-1-chloroethane  iii) ethoxyethane  iv) 2-aminopropanoic acid
blocks.explanation:
To draw a mirror image: draw the central carbon with its four groups in 3D (two in the plane, one wedge forward, one dash back), then draw the same molecule as seen in a mirror, with left and right reversed.
i) 2-bromo-2-chloropropane, (CH₃)₂CBrCl: C-2 carries two identical CH₃ groups; the mirror image can be turned to fit on the original → achiral.
ii) 1-bromo-1-chloroethane, CH₃CHBrCl: C-1 carries H, CH₃, Br and Cl (four different) → chiral; the molecule and its mirror image are a pair of enantiomers.
iii) Ethoxyethane, CH₃CH₂–O–CH₂CH₃: no carbon has four different groups and the molecule has a plane of symmetry → achiral.
iv) 2-Aminopropanoic acid, CH₃CH(NH₂)COOH: C-2 carries H, CH₃, NH₂ and COOH → chiral; it exists as two enantiomers.

blocks.prompt: c) What is the alkane of lowest relative molecular mass that contains a chiral centre? Give its systematic name and molecular formula. Also draw mirror image of this compound.
blocks.explanation:
A chiral carbon needs four different groups; in an alkane the smallest set is H, CH₃, C₂H₅ and C₃H₇, which needs 7 carbons.
Name: 3-methylhexane, CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₃
Molecular formula: C₇H₁₆ (Mr = 100); C-3 is chiral (H, CH₃, C₂H₅, CH₂CH₂CH₃).
Mirror image: draw C-3 with H, CH₃, C₂H₅ and C₃H₇ in 3D and reflect it: the two forms are non-superimposable enantiomers.
(2,3-Dimethylpentane, also C₇H₁₆, has a chiral C-3 as well.)

blocks.prompt: d) 3-chlorobutan-2-ol is an optically active compound. Draw all its possible optical isomers. Is there any meso form of this compound? Give reason.
blocks.explanation:
CH₃–CH(OH)–CH(Cl)–CH₃ has two chiral carbons: C-2 (H, OH, CH₃, CHClCH₃) and C-3 (H, Cl, CH₃, CH(OH)CH₃).
Number of optical isomers = 2ⁿ = 2² = 4.
Drawn with the chain vertical (CH₃ at the top, C-2, C-3, CH₃ at the bottom), H and the other group on the sides:
Isomer 1: OH on the right at C-2, Cl on the right at C-3
Isomer 2: OH on the left, Cl on the left (mirror image of 1)
Isomer 3: OH on the right, Cl on the left
Isomer 4: OH on the left, Cl on the right (mirror image of 3)
So there are two pairs of enantiomers (1, 2) and (3, 4).
Meso form: none. A meso form needs two similar chiral carbons so that one half of the molecule is the mirror image of the other. Here C-2 carries OH and C-3 carries Cl, so the two halves are never alike, no isomer has a plane of symmetry, and all four isomers are optically active.

blocks.prompt: Q4. Explain the difference between homolytic and heterolytic fissions of a covalent bond.
blocks.explanation:
A covalent bond can break in two ways.
Homolytic fission (homolysis): occurs when the breaking bond is nonpolar. The two shared electrons are divided equally, one to each atom, giving atoms or groups with unpaired electrons, called free radicals:
Cl–Cl → Cl• + •Cl (in sunlight or on heating)
Free radicals are very reactive intermediates and lead to free radical mechanisms, e.g. chlorination of methane.
Heterolytic fission (heterolysis): occurs when the breaking bond is polar. The shared pair goes to the more electronegative atom, which becomes negative; the other atom becomes positive:
CH₃–Cl → CH₃⁺ + Cl⁻
When carbon is bonded to a more electronegative atom (O, N, halogen) a carbocation forms; when it is bonded to a less electronegative metal (Li, Mg) a carbanion forms. Heterolysis gives electrophiles and nucleophiles and leads to ionic (polar) mechanisms.

rows: Occurs in a nonpolar bond
Occurs in a polar bond
Shared pair divided equally, one electron to each atom
Shared pair goes to one atom (the more electronegative)
Gives free radicals (unpaired electrons)
Gives ions: a cation and an anion (e.g. carbocation)
e.g. Cl–Cl → Cl• + •Cl (sunlight)
e.g. CH₃–Cl → CH₃⁺ + Cl⁻
Leads to free radical mechanisms
Leads to ionic (polar) mechanisms

blocks.prompt: Q5. Discuss cis-trans isomerism. Explain with two examples.
blocks.explanation:
Cis-trans isomers are stereoisomers that have a different spatial arrangement of groups because rotation about a double bond is restricted (open-chain compounds).
Reason: around a C–C single bond groups rotate freely, but a C=C bond is a σ bond plus a π bond formed by sideways overlap of p orbitals. The π bond locks the two sp² carbons and their groups in one plane; rotating would break it (about 263 kJ mol⁻¹), which is not possible at room temperature.
Cis isomer: two similar groups on the same side of the double bond. Trans isomer: on opposite sides.
Condition: the molecule must have a double bond, and each doubly bonded carbon must carry two different groups. So but-1-ene (CH₂=) and 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene ((CH₃)₂C=) show no cis-trans isomerism.
Example 1: but-2-ene, CH₃–CH=CH–CH₃: cis-but-2-ene (both CH₃ on the same side) and trans-but-2-ene (CH₃ on opposite sides).
Example 2: 1,2-dichloroethene, ClCH=CHCl: cis (both Cl on the same side, polar) and trans (Cl opposite, dipoles cancel, non-polar).
Properties: cis and trans isomers differ in melting point, boiling point, dipole moment, density and heat of vaporization; trans isomers are more stable than cis.

blocks.prompt: Q6. Describe the phenomenon of optical activity. Explain with an example.
blocks.explanation:
Optical activity is the ability of a substance to rotate the plane of plane-polarized light (PPL: monochromatic light vibrating in one plane). It is detected and measured with a polarimeter: a solution of the compound is placed in the path of PPL; if the plane is rotated the compound is optically active.
Dextrorotatory (+): rotates the plane to the right (clockwise). Laevorotatory (−): rotates it to the left (anticlockwise).
Condition: the molecule must be non-superimposable on its mirror image (chiral), like our left and right hands. A carbon atom bonded to four different groups is a chiral carbon; a molecule with one chiral carbon is always optically active. Molecules superimposable on their mirror images are achiral and inactive.
Example: lactic acid, CH₃–CH(OH)–COOH. The central carbon is chiral (bonded to H, OH, CH₃ and COOH). It has two non-superimposable mirror-image forms (enantiomers): (+)-lactic acid and (−)-lactic acid. They have identical properties but rotate PPL equally in opposite directions; a 50 : 50 mixture is the optically inactive racemic mixture (±)-lactic acid.
Maximum number of optical isomers = 2ⁿ (n = number of chiral carbons).

blocks.prompt: Q7. What is the difference between racemic mixture and meso compound? Draw the structures of enantiomers and meso form of lactic acid.
blocks.explanation:
Racemic mixture: an equimolar mixture of the (+) and (−) enantiomers; optically inactive because the rotation by one enantiomer is cancelled by the other (external compensation), e.g. (±)-lactic acid.
Meso compound: a single stereoisomer with at least two similar chiral carbons and a plane of symmetry; optically inactive because one half of the molecule cancels the rotation of the other half (internal compensation), e.g. meso-tartaric acid.
Enantiomers of lactic acid, CH₃CH(OH)COOH (in words): the chiral carbon with H, OH, CH₃ and COOH arranged tetrahedrally; in one form, with COOH at the top and CH₃ at the bottom, OH is on the right and H on the left; the other form is its mirror image, OH on the left and H on the right. These are (+)- and (−)-lactic acid.
Meso form: lactic acid has only one chiral carbon, so it has no meso form (see the Book correction). The meso form is shown by tartaric acid, HOOC–CH(OH)–CH(OH)–COOH: with both COOH groups vertical, both OH groups are on the same side, so a plane of symmetry passes between the two chiral carbons.

rows: Mixture of two compounds: equal (50 : 50) amounts of (+) and (−) enantiomers
A single compound (one stereoisomer)
Optically inactive by external compensation (one molecule cancels another)
Optically inactive by internal compensation (one half cancels the other half)
Can be separated (resolved) into the two active enantiomers
Cannot be separated into active forms
Possible with one chiral carbon, e.g. (±)-lactic acid
Needs at least two similar chiral carbons and a plane of symmetry, e.g. meso-tartaric acid
Written with (±)
Has a plane of symmetry in the molecule

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Lactic acid, CH₃CH(OH)COOH, has only one chiral carbon, so it cannot have a meso form; it exists only as (+) and (−) enantiomers and their racemic mixture, as the chapter itself says. A meso form needs at least two similar chiral carbons; the chapter's example is tartaric acid, whose meso form is described in the answer.
